title: Hoe oud ben je?
goal: Count from 0 to 100, ask and say someone's age with zijn, say and understand a Dutch phone number, and spell a name with the Dutch letter names.

content: It is Saturday morning, 5 September, Sofia's first weekend in Utrecht. She still has her Spanish phone (
) and wants a Dutch number, so she goes to a phone shop (
) in the centre, where a shop assistant (
) helps her. In this lesson you will learn the Dutch numbers from 0 to 100, say how old you are, give a phone number, and spell your name.

words.note: telefoon + winkel, written as one word (like vrijdagmiddagborrel, 03-b).

content: and the new forms of this lesson are bold. A wrong form is shown like

content.text: Saturday morning. Sofia is in a phone shop in the centre of Utrecht.

nog meant 'still' in 03-b; here it means 'again'.
een is 'a/an' and the unstressed 'one'; één is written with accents when the number must stand out, as in a phone number read digit by digit.

blocks.content: Dutch numbers are mostly regular, but 21–99 go in a surprising order, and a few numbers have small spelling traps. Learn them well: you will use them for ages, phone numbers and, later, prices.

content: (11, 12) by heart. 13–19 are a unit + tien, but three have a spelling trap: it is
the unit is der-, not drie-
the unit is veer-, not vier-
The tens follow the same pattern:
(40) also use der- and veer-, and
is 100: Dutch just says honderd, with no een in front.
From 21 to 99, Dutch says the unit first, then
, then the ten, all as one word:
. English goes the other way ("twenty-one"), and so does Spanish ("veintiuno"), which is why Spanish speakers sometimes say
After twee and drie the en gets two dots (a trema):
. The dots show that a new syllable starts (twee-en-twin-tig), just like in België (02-a). Without them it is wrong:
. No trema anywhere else: vierentwintig, vijfentwintig.
Add en (ën after twee or drie: tweeën-, drieën-).
Write it all as one word: eenentwintig, tweeëntwintig.
. After twee and drie, en gets a trema:

props.translation: Twenty-one, twenty-two, thirty-three.
props.note: The trema (ë) comes only after twee and drie.

props.translation: Sixty-four is 64. Forty-six is 46.
props.note: A common mix-up: the unit always comes first (vier + en + zestig).

content: (informal), Hoe oud bent u? (formal), Hoe oud is Daan? Answer: Ik ben achtentwintig. / Ik ben 28
. The word jaar (year) stays singular after a number: 28 jaar, never

) is an adjective after zijn: Ik ben oud! Achtentwintig is niet oud. To correct a wrong guess, give the right fact, with no niet before the number: Ben jij zevenentwintig? — Nee, ik ben achtentwintig.

words.note: stays singular right after a number: 28 jaar.
jaar is optional: Ik ben 28. / Ik ben 28 jaar.

content: Dutch uses zijn for age, not hebben, and jaar stays singular after a number.
→ Ik ben 28 jaar (zijn, not hebben; hebben comes in 04-b). Also:

props.translation: How old are you? — I'm twenty-eight.
props.note: ben jij loses its t (01-b, 03-b). Also fine: Ik ben 28 jaar.

content: and have eight more digits, written 06-38221974 or 06 38 22 19 74. People say them
after 06 (nul zes, achtendertig, tweeëntwintig, negentien, vierenzeventig) or

(nul zes, drie acht, twee twee, één negen, zeven vier). Both are normal, and 0 is always nul. Utrecht landlines start with 030 (nul dertig); the emergency number is 112, said één één twee. When it goes too fast: Pardon? Nog een keer, alstublieft. Langzaam, alstublieft. Giving your own number:

words.note: mijn as a chunk (possessives come in 05-a).

blocks.content: Dutch mobile numbers always start with 06; Utrecht's area code is 030. The emergency number is 112, said digit by digit: één één twee. Asking a friend's or colleague's age is normal in the Netherlands, but people rarely ask an older stranger Hoe oud bent u?

props.translation: 112: one one two.
props.note: The emergency number, always said digit by digit.

props.translation: My number is now 06-38221974.
props.note: nu recycles 02-b. Say it: nul zes, achtendertig, tweeëntwintig, negentien, vierenzeventig.

props.note: A short form, as in the phone shop. de leeftijd = age.

words.note: Mijn naam is … was a chunk in 01-a; naam is now its own word.

content: ) as English, but the letter names sound different. The vowels' names are their long sounds: Dutch e sounds like English "A", Dutch i like English "E". Asking someone to spell:
(informal) / Hoe schrijft u dat? (formal). Answering: the letters one by one (Moreno: em – oo – er – ee – en – oo).
: Je schrijft Utrecht met een hoofdletter. Names: Mijn
is Moreno. Compounds such as telefoonwinkel, telefoonnummer and simkaart are written as one word. When spelling, Dutch people call the letters ij and ei by name:
): schrijven has the lange ij, klein has the korte ei. Learn these two names as fixed names only.

words.meaning: 'long ij' / 'short ei': the names of the letters ij and ei when you spell
words.note: Two fixed letter names only, not a model for adjective + noun (06-b).

content: – ij, or i-grec / griekse ij (like ij)

blocks.content: The vowels' letter names are their long sounds: a "aa", e "ee" (English "A"!), i "ie" (English "E"!), o "oo", u "uu". g is "gee" and j is "jee" ("yay"). Second sound: -tig in twintig, dertig, veertig ends in the throat g/ch from 01-a ("twin-tich"), and the stress is on the first part: TWIN-tig, but EEN-en-twin-tig.

content: , said short and unstressed ("un"). When it clearly means the number one, write
and stress it ("ayn"): één woord, één negen.

props.translation: You write Utrecht with a capital letter.
props.note: je here means people in general. Cities, countries and languages always take a capital letter.

props.translation: "Telefoonwinkel" is one word.
props.note: één, with accents, because it clearly means the number one.

props.translation: My first name is Sofia. My surname is Moreno.
props.note: mijn as a chunk (01-a).

props.translation: How do you spell that? — N-O-O-R.
props.note: schrijf je loses its t (03-b). Noor has a double o: say oo twice.

content.text: Late morning. Sofia is back at Noor's flat. Noor works in the café later today.

blocks.content: Sofia's message to the team chat on Saturday morning, written from the phone shop. She makes one spelling mistake (telefoon winkel), and Daan corrects it in the next message.

data.instruction: Read the team chat and answer in Dutch; short answers are fine. Waar is …? = Where is …?; Hoe zeg je …? = How do you say …?; Hoe schrijf je …? = How do you spell …?; Wie schrijft …? = Who writes …?; Klopt dit? = Is this right? Example: Wie schrijft “Super!”? → Daan.

passage.title: Mijn nummer is nu …
passage.content:
Sofia: Hoi allemaal! Ik ben in het centrum, in een telefoon winkel. Mijn nummer is nu 06-38221974. Groetjes, Sofia
Daan: Hoi Sofia! Super! Nul zes, achtendertig, tweeëntwintig, negentien, vierenzeventig?
Sofia: Ja, precies!
Daan: Heel goed! En “telefoonwinkel” is één woord: t-e-l-e-f-o-o-n-w-i-n-k-e-l.
Sofia: Oké, dank je! Nederlands is moeilijk!
Karin: Nee hoor, je schrijft heel goed Nederlands! Ik ben thuis, in Amersfoort. Groetjes, Karin

data.instruction: Write 2–4 short sentences: your name and how to spell it, your age, and a phone number (you may invent one).

authorsVersion: Ik heet Sofia Moreno. Moreno: M-O-R-E-N-O. Ik ben achtentwintig jaar. Mijn nummer is 06-38221974.
items.note: Model answer by Sofia. Also fine: Mijn achternaam is …; digits or words for the age; no real phone number needed.

blocks.content: 0–20: learn elf, twaalf by heart; watch dertien, veertien, achttien.
Tens: twintig, dertig, veertig … tachtig, negentig, honderd.
21–99: unit + en + ten, one word (eenentwintig); a trema after twee and drie (tweeëntwintig).
Hoe oud ben je? — Ik ben 28 (jaar): zijn, not hebben; jaar stays singular.
Phone numbers: 06 + eight digits, in pairs or digit by digit; Pardon? Nog een keer, alstublieft.
Hoe schrijf je dat? — spell with the Dutch letter names (e = “ee”, i = “ie”).

extras: the Verkoper, a young man in his early twenties with short curly black hair and a dark-blue shop polo shirt
